title: MB2-00570
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, is alleging that he is a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), that he has a well-founded fear of persecution and that he would be subjected to a "risk to [his] life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment," as well as to a danger of torture, should he have to return to his country, under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The claimant alleges that he was a member of the Union pour la démocratie et le progrès social (UDPS) [union for democracy and social progress] and that he was in charge of awareness and recruitment in his neighbourhood in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He participated in a march on XXXX XXXX, 2011, and he was arrested and mistreated in detention. Three or four days later, he fled the place of detention with assistance from one of the police officers. He lived in hiding for three months because he was wanted by the authorities. The claimant left on XXXX XXXX, 2011, for the United States, where he stayed until XXXX XXXX, 2012, the date he arrived in Canada.
After examining all the testimonial and documentary evidence, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection."
The determinative issue is the credibility of the claimant's allegations. Identity

Given that a copy of a voter's card and of a driver's licence were submitted, and that the panel did not receive information casting doubt on their genuineness, the panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity.1 Credibility
The claimant was not credible and his testimony was not trustworthy with respect to the essential elements of his refugee protection claim, for the following reasons, among others.

The claimant testified that he joined the UDPS in XXXX 2011. When asked why he had not submitted a membership card for that party, the claimant testified that his card had been taken when he was arrested in XXXX 2011 and that he had not received a new card. When asked whether he had taken steps to obtain another, the claimant testified that he had contacted his sister in the DRC but that she had been unable to obtain one for him. When asked why he had not taken steps with the UDPS, the claimant testified that he did not see the importance of having a card, that politics no longer interested him and that he did not know that the UDPS was in Canada.

The panel is not satisfied as to these explanations. The panel considers it reasonable to believe that if the claimant had been a member of the UDPS, and his sister had been unable to obtain a card for him, he would have taken other steps to obtain a membership card or documentary evidence to support his alleged membership. According to documentary evidence,2 this card may be obtained by contacting the section or cell to which the individual belongs. In addition, in Canada, UDPS/Canada facilitates obtaining the card by, among other things, making inquiries with the UDPS in the DRC to confirm whether or not the individual was a member. The panel is of the opinion that, through his apparent lack of steps with the UDPS to obtain such documentary evidence, the claimant did not establish that he was a member of the UDPS. This undermines the claimant's credibility.

When asked about the motto of the UDPS, the claimant stated that it was [translation] "Hold on, the UDPS will win." When asked about the UDPS hymn, the claimant testified that it was in Lingala and that he did not know the title. When confronted with the documentary evidence,3 that the motto and hymn were not those that he had mentioned, the claimant responded that they were what he had heard during the demonstrations. In addition, after the break, the claimant's lawyer alleged that the claimant used to have XXXX XXXX and that if he was stressed, he could hesitate.

The panel is not satisfied as to these explanations. The panel considers it reasonable to believe that if the claimant was a member of the UDPS, in addition to submitting a membership card, he also would have testified spontaneously and without contradiction about this basic information, such as the party's motto and hymn. Moreover, if the claimant allegedly had problems testifying because he used to XXXX, the panel considers it reasonable to believe that this [translation] "difficulty" would also have been reflected in his entire testimony. In addition, the panel is of the opinion that he would have known the UDPS motto and hymn. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant's explanations are insufficient to explain the contradictions noted and his lack of knowledge about this basic information. This reinforces the panel's conclusion not to believe that the claimant was a member of the UDPS.

The claimant testified that he had promoted awareness and done recruitment in XXXX 2011. When asked what he had done for recruitment, he testified that he had contacted young people in his neighbourhood and that he had recruited about ten people. When asked whether he could be more specific regarding the manner in which he had recruited them, the claimant repeated the same explanations.

The panel considers it reasonable to believe that if the claimant had done recruitment for the UDPS, he would have testified spontaneously and he would have provided details about these recruitment efforts, which was not the case. In addition, given the importance of this allegation, the panel considers it reasonable to believe that the claimant would have taken steps to obtain documentary evidence to support his statements. For all these reasons, the panel does not believe that he was doing recruitment. This reinforces the panel's conclusion that the claimant did not establish his membership in the UDPS. Consequently, the panel does not believe that the claimant was imprisoned and mistreated because of an alleged membership in the UDPS.

For all these reasons, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not establish a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture should he return to his country.
For all these reasons, after considering all the oral and documentary evidence, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection."

The panel rejects the claim of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
